headline: 13-year-old builds software company Akhouri Systems, shares lessons from 1 month of development
summary: Akhouri Anmol Kumar, a 13-year-old from India, founded Akhouri Systems and built multiple apps. He shares insights from his first month, including gaining 120 downloads without prior recommendations.
details: Akhouri Anmol Kumar, a 13-year-old from India, has founded Akhouri Systems. In just one month, he developed several applications and garnered 120 downloads from strangers, all without any prior recommendations or marketing.
Kumar emphasizes a philosophy of 'shipped > perfect,' constantly improving his apps through updates rather than waiting for an ideal version. He notes that nothing ships if one waits for perfection.

His motivation for building apps stems from personal frustrations with existing tools. He developed ANOTE to replace outdated Windows Notepad, ATLOCK for a more secure app locker, ACALCU with 30+ themes for boring calculators, and APIC for messy image tools.

While building the software was challenging, Kumar found that getting people to discover his existence was the harder part. Despite this, the organic downloads motivate him significantly more than view counts.
Kumar started his venture without a degree, a mentor, or external funding, proving that passion and initiative can overcome traditional barriers in the tech world.

headline_marked: [[Google Paid $2.7B to Keep Its Best AI Researcher]]. He Left Anyway.
headline: Google Paid $2.7B to Keep Its Best AI Researcher. He Left Anyway.
summary: Noam Shazeer, the inventor of the transformer architecture and co-lead of Google's Gemini, left for OpenAI after Google paid $2.7 billion to buy him back from Character.AI. This highlights a broader talent drain from Google DeepMind.
details: Google paid $2.7 billion to bring Noam Shazeer back in 2024. Shazeer, who invented the transformer architecture—the foundation for GPT, Gemini, and Claude—has now joined OpenAI. This move follows a pattern of top Google DeepMind researchers departing for AI startups.

Other notable departures include John Jumper, co-creator of AlphaFold and Nobel laureate, who left for Anthropic. Ruoming Pang, hired by Meta for $200 million to lead their Superintelligence team, jumped to OpenAI after just seven months.

The core issue isn't compensation, as Google pays well, but rather a lack of autonomy. The Los Angeles Times reported that researchers are frustrated by a "compute crunch"—intense internal competition for GPU access, slowing down research and innovation.

Startups offer more freedom, allowing researchers to quickly experiment and iterate without bureaucratic hurdles. Additionally, startup equity, especially with companies like OpenAI targeting a $1 trillion IPO valuation, presents a potentially far greater financial incentive than Google's RSUs.

Despite the talent exodus, Google's AI products remain strong, with Gemini 2.5 being competitive and DeepMind continuing to publish breakthrough research. Accenture recently expanded its partnership with Google Cloud for enterprise AI using Gemini.

The long-term question is whether Google's product momentum and massive scale can withstand this significant brain drain. The departure of key figures like Shazeer and Jumper, who developed foundational AI technologies, raises concerns about the future of Google's AI leadership.
